gaps/codes: An autoencoder squeezes each image into a short code, z, and its decoder rebuilds the image from it. Picture a code of one number: each image is a point on a line.
gaps/new: Can the decoder make new images? Decode a code that no image produced, between the seven and the zero.
gaps/smudge: Out comes a smudge: training only ever showed the decoder the codes of real images, so between them it learned nothing.
gaps/cloud: The fix: give each image a range of codes, and train the decoder to rebuild it from anywhere in that range. Wide enough, the ranges cover the gaps.
spread/bell: The range is a bell curve. Draw many random numbers, as for a network's first weights, and count how often each value comes up: most near the middle, fewer farther out. That pattern is a distribution.
spread/mu: The encoder places a bell for each image. First, its center: the mean, written mu, the Greek letter mu. Here, one.
spread/sigma: Then its width: the standard deviation, sigma, here a half. A spread, not the sigmoid. A width cannot be negative, so e to the x makes it positive.
spread/four: A code of two numbers gets two bells, so the encoder outputs four numbers, each with its own row of weights and its own bias.
spread/name: Diederik Kingma and Max Welling introduced this in 2013: the variational autoencoder, or V A E. Variational methods, from statistics, replace a distribution too hard to compute with the closest simple one. Here, a bell.
sample/eps: To train, draw a code from the bell. Start with noise from the standard normal, mean zero and standard deviation one: epsilon, the Greek letter epsilon, here zero point four.
sample/stretch: Stretch it by the spread: sigma times epsilon, a half times zero point four, is zero point two.
sample/shift: Then shift it by the mean: one plus zero point two, so z is one point two. The second dimension gives minus zero point seven.
sample/fresh: Each training step draws fresh noise, so a fresh code under the bell, and the decoder must rebuild this same image from every one.
sample/grad: The randomness sits in epsilon, which no weight sets, so backprop passes through z to mu and sigma: z moves one for one with mu, and epsilon times as fast as sigma.
sample/trick: Kingma and Welling called this the reparameterization trick: random draw and all, the model trains with ordinary gradient steps.
pull/cheat: With only the reconstruction error, the autoencoder's squared error, a V A E would cheat: shrink every sigma to zero, and the noise is gone. One exact code per image again, gaps and all.
pull/term: So the loss adds a term per code dimension, comparing its bell with the standard normal: zero when they match, mu zero and sigma one.
pull/mean: Set the mean at two, and mu squared, halved, makes the term two. That pulls every mean toward zero.
pull/narrow: Narrow the bell to sigma a half, and minus the log of sigma squared climbs, since the log of a number below one is negative: about zero point three two.
pull/wide: Widen it to sigma two, and sigma squared, the variance, takes over: about zero point eight one. Lowest at exactly one, it pulls every spread toward one.
pull/kl: This is the K L divergence, from Solomon Kullback and Richard Leibler in 1951: a measure of how much one distribution differs from another.
pull/generate: Pulled toward one bell, the images' bells overlap and fill the standard normal. So draw any code from it, decode it, and out comes a new image.
